title: React fundamentals
blurb: Components, props, state, keys, rendering. The questions asked before anyone opens your portfolio. Code assumes React 19 with createRoot and StrictMode off, unless the question says otherwise.

questions.q: What is the `key` prop for?
choices: It is required by the linter but has no effect once the app is running
It sets the element's DOM `id`, so CSS and tests can select each item
It identifies a list item across renders so React can match it to its state
It sets the order in which sibling components are rendered and then mounted
questions.why: Without stable keys React matches list items by position. Delete the first row and every later row's state shifts up one: inputs keep the wrong values, checkboxes tick the wrong items. Keys never reach the DOM.
questions.asked: Universal. The strong answer describes the bug bad keys cause, not just the rule.

questions.q: When is using the array index as a key acceptable?
choices: When the list is never reordered, filtered, or added to except at the end
Always, because an index is a stable number that never repeats in a list
Never: React throws a warning and refuses to render index-keyed lists
Whenever the list is short, since reconciliation cost is what keys fix
questions.why: The index is only stable if positions are stable. A static list rendered once is fine; anything sortable, filterable or deletable needs a real id. Keys are about matching state to items, not about speed on long lists.
questions.asked: It tests whether you know the rule's reason well enough to know when it can be broken.

questions.q: What renders when `items` is an empty array?
choices: Nothing inside the div
An empty List component
An error: `0` is not a node
A literal 0 on the page
questions.why: `0 && ...` evaluates to `0`, and React renders numbers; it skips only booleans, `null` and `undefined`. Use `items.length > 0 && ...` or a ternary.
questions.asked: A tiny bug that ships to production constantly, so it is a quick filter question.

questions.q: What does this log on a single click, and what does `count` become?
choices: 0, and count becomes 2
0, and count becomes 1
1, and count becomes 2
2, and count becomes 2
questions.why: `count` is a constant captured by this render, so both calls set it to 0 + 1. The log shows the old value because setting state does not change the current render's variables. `setCount(c => c + 1)` twice would give 2.
questions.asked: The single best question for finding out whether someone understands React's render model.

questions.q: Why can this fail to update the screen?
choices: `push` throws in StrictMode, because state arrays are frozen in development builds
React compares references, so the same array looks unchanged and it may skip the render
The mutation corrupts the virtual DOM, so React has to discard the component tree
It updates fine; not mutating state is a style convention from the Redux era
questions.why: React bails out when `Object.is(prev, next)` is true, and a mutated array is still the same reference. `setTodos([...todos, newTodo])` gives React something new to compare. React does not freeze state, so nothing throws.
questions.asked: Constant. It links directly to the JavaScript reference-equality question.

questions.q: What is the difference between props and state?
choices: State holds objects and arrays; props hold primitives such as strings and numbers
Props trigger a re-render when they change; state changes never re-render
State is shared across the whole app; props are local to a single component
Props are passed in and read-only; state is owned and updated by the component
questions.why: If a value comes from above and the component never changes it, it is a prop. If the component owns it over time, it is state. If it can be computed from either, it should be neither: derive it during render.
questions.asked: The opener for most React screens; the derive-it-instead point is what lifts the answer.

questions.q: What is wrong with this?
choices: `count` is derived state; compute `items.length` during render
The dependency array should be `[items.length]`, not `[items]`
`setCount` cannot be called inside an effect without a guard
The effect needs a cleanup function that resets `count` to 0
questions.why: Storing derived state adds an extra render, a moment where the two disagree, and a synchronisation bug waiting to happen. Narrowing the dependency still keeps the redundant state. Anything computable from existing state or props should be computed.
questions.asked: One of the 'you might not need an effect' patterns from the React docs, asked often.

questions.q: What does 'lifting state up' mean?
choices: Moving component state into a global store so that any component can read it
Moving state into a context provider at the root of the application
Moving shared state to the closest common ancestor of the components using it
Moving state from a child into props, so that the child becomes a pure function
questions.why: Two siblings that must agree cannot each own the value, so the nearest ancestor owns it and passes down the value plus a setter. A global store or root context is a bigger move than needed; colocation says keep state as low as it can go.
questions.asked: It checks you reach for the smallest fix before a store or context.

questions.q: What is a controlled input?
choices: An input whose `required` and `pattern` rules are enforced by React
An input inside a `<form>`, so React manages its submission for you
An input rendered with `readOnly`, so users cannot change its value
An input whose value comes from state, updated through `onChange`
questions.why: Controlled means React state is the single source of truth, so you can format, validate or reset as the user types. Uncontrolled leaves the value in the DOM and you read it at submit: lighter, and fine for simple forms.
questions.asked: It usually leads into 'when would you choose uncontrolled?', which shows real form experience.

questions.q: What happens if you pass `value` without `onChange` to a text input?
choices: It works normally, and React reads the new value back on submit
The component throws on the first keystroke the user makes
The field cannot be edited, and React logs a warning about it
React silently switches it to an uncontrolled input instead
questions.why: React re-renders with the same `value` after every keystroke, so nothing typed appears, and it warns in development. Use `defaultValue` for an uncontrolled field, or add the `onChange` handler.
questions.asked: Everyone has hit the 'I can't type in my input' bug; this checks you know why.

questions.q: What is the virtual DOM, and why does React use one?
choices: A faster reimplementation of the browser DOM, used instead of the real one
A description of the UI that React diffs to work out the real DOM changes
A copy of the page kept in a Web Worker so rendering is off the main thread
A browser API that React polyfills in browsers which do not support it
questions.why: The value is not raw speed: hand-written DOM code is faster. The value is that you write `render(state)` declaratively and React works out the imperative steps. It lives on the main thread in ordinary JavaScript objects.
questions.asked: The wrong answer is 'because it's faster than the DOM'.

questions.q: When does a component re-render?
choices: When its state changes, its parent renders, or its context changes
Only when one of its props changes value, compared deeply
On every animation frame while the component is mounted
Only when the component calls `forceUpdate` or `setState`
questions.why: A parent rendering re-renders its children by default, whether or not their props changed; that is what `React.memo` opts out of. Re-rendering does not mean a DOM update; the diff may produce nothing.
questions.asked: The 'parent renders, child renders' default is the root of most React performance questions.

questions.q: Why does the input lose what you typed whenever `Parent` re-renders?
choices: `Child` needs a `key`, or React cannot match it between renders
An `<input>` cannot keep state unless it is a controlled input
`Child` is a new function each render, so React remounts it
`Child` is not wrapped in `memo`, so its state resets on render
questions.why: A new function on each render is a new component type, so React unmounts the old tree and mounts a fresh one: state gone, input cleared, effects re-run. A key or `memo` does not help because the type itself changes. Define components at module level.
questions.asked: A bug people hit when they extract a component 'for tidiness' inside another.

questions.q: How do you reset a child's internal state when a prop, such as `userId`, changes?
choices: Render the child with `key={userId}`
Call `setState` in an effect that depends on `userId`
Call `forceUpdate` on the child when `userId` changes
Wrap the child in `memo` with `userId` as a dependency
questions.why: A new key makes React treat it as a different instance, so it unmounts and remounts with fresh state. The effect works but renders once with stale state first. This is the documented alternative.
questions.asked: A neat trick that shows you have read the docs rather than only Stack Overflow.

questions.q: What is JSX, mechanically?
choices: A template language that React parses and interprets at runtime
HTML embedded in JavaScript and inserted as a string of markup
A browser-native syntax that React enables with a polyfill
Syntax compiled to function calls that create plain element objects
questions.why: `<Foo bar={1} />` compiles to a call producing `{ type: Foo, props: { bar: 1 } }`. That is why components must be capitalised: lowercase compiles to the string `'foo'`, not a reference. Nothing is parsed at runtime.
questions.asked: Knowing JSX is just function calls explains keys, capitalisation and why `if` cannot sit inside it.

questions.q: Why must hooks be called unconditionally at the top level?
choices: It is a lint convention only; React itself works with conditional hooks
React tracks hooks by call order, so a skipped call shifts later hooks
Conditional hooks run slower, because React cannot cache their results
Function hoisting moves hooks to the top, so conditions are ignored
questions.why: No name is attached to a hook, only its position in the call sequence. Skip one on a later render and the second `useState` reads the state belonging to the first. It is a correctness rule, not a performance one.
questions.asked: The good answer explains the mechanism rather than reciting 'the rules of hooks'.

questions.q: When should you use `useReducer` instead of `useState`?
choices: Whenever a component holds more than one piece of state at a time
When several values change together or transitions have real logic
Only when the app already uses Redux, so actions stay consistent
Whenever the state is an object rather than a primitive value
questions.why: A reducer moves the transition logic out of handlers into one pure function you can test on its own. For a wizard or a form with interdependent fields it is far clearer than five setters; for two unrelated values it is ceremony.
questions.asked: It tests judgement: a reducer everywhere is as much a smell as none at all.

questions.q: What does `user.age` show after the second click?
choices: 2, because the spread copies stale state
1, because objects never re-render
2, because updates to objects batch
3, because each click sees fresh state
questions.why: Each render closes over that render's state, and the second click happens after the re-render, so `user` is current. The stale-closure problem appears only when a handler is captured once: in an effect, a timer or a memoised callback.
questions.asked: It separates real stale-closure bugs from the imagined ones people add `prev =>` everywhere to avoid.

questions.q: What is 'colocating state'?
choices: Keeping state in the lowest component that needs it
Keeping all application state in one file so it is easy to find
Keeping state next to the CSS module whose styles it affects
Keeping shared state in context instead of passing it as props
questions.why: State lifted higher than necessary re-renders the whole subtree on every keystroke. Pushing it down is often a bigger performance win than any amount of `memo`, and it costs nothing.
questions.asked: The correct first answer to 'how would you fix a slow React page?'.

questions.q: An element keeps the same type and key at the same position between renders. What does React do?
choices: Unmounts it and mounts a fresh instance with the new props
Replaces its DOM node but carries the component state across to it
Keeps the DOM node and state, updating only the changed props
Warns about a duplicate key and renders both of the elements
questions.why: Reconciliation preserves the instance when type and key match at the same position. Change the type or the key and React tears down and rebuilds, losing state and re-running effects.
questions.asked: It is the rule underneath keys, remount bugs and the key-reset trick.

questions.q: Why does React batch several `setState` calls from one event into one render?
choices: So the calls run in the order they were made, which it could not otherwise do
So each render uses less memory, since fewer fibers are allocated at once
So server requests fired from the handler cannot race with each other
So the UI never shows a half-applied update and renders only once
questions.why: Three setters in one handler produce one render, so the screen never shows an intermediate state where one value changed and its partner did not, and no work is wasted. Since React 18 this also covers promises, timeouts and native handlers ('automatic batching').
questions.asked: The follow-up is usually 'what changed in React 18?', which is automatic batching.

questions.q: Which update to one list item is correct without mutating any existing state?
choices: `items[index].done = true; setItems([...items])`
`setItems(items.splice(index, 1, updated))`
`setItems(items.map(i => i.id === id ? { ...i, done: true } : i))`
`items.find(i => i.id === id).done = true; setItems([...items])`
questions.why: `map` gives a new array and a new object for the changed row, leaving the rest referentially identical, so memoised rows do not re-render. The spread options make a new array but still mutate the shared item object; `splice` mutates and returns the removed items.
questions.asked: A practical check: it needs both immutability and referential-equality reasoning.

questions.q: What is a fragment (`<>...</>`) for?
choices: Rendering its children only when a condition is true
Returning several elements without an extra DOM wrapper
Lazy-loading a subtree the first time that it is rendered
Grouping props so they can be spread onto children
questions.why: It avoids the 'div soup' that breaks CSS grid and flex layouts and table markup. Use `<Fragment key={id}>` when you need a key on it, since the short syntax cannot take props.
questions.asked: A warm-up; the key-on-a-fragment detail shows you have used it inside lists.

questions.q: What does `<StrictMode>` do in a production build?
choices: Nothing: its extra renders and effect re-runs are development-only
It double-renders components, but no longer re-runs any effects
It re-runs every effect once, to catch cleanups missing in prod
It throws on deprecated APIs instead of just logging a warning
questions.why: StrictMode's double render and mount-unmount-mount effect cycle exist to surface impure renders and missing cleanups while you develop; production builds skip them. So 'my fetch runs twice' in development is not a production bug, but the missing cleanup it reveals is.
questions.asked: It stops candidates 'fixing' StrictMode double effects with a ref guard that hides real bugs.

questions.q: How should a child tell its parent that something changed?
choices: By mutating the prop object, which the parent still holds
By dispatching a custom DOM event for the parent to hear
By calling a callback the parent passed down as a prop
By writing the value to a module-level shared variable
questions.why: Data flows down, events flow up. The parent owns the state and passes both the value and the updater, which keeps a single source of truth. Mutating a prop changes nothing React can see, so nothing re-renders.
questions.asked: The one-way data flow question every React screen includes in some form.

questions.q: What is wrong with this event handler?
choices: It calls `handleClick` during render and uses its return value
It must be `onclick`, because React mirrors the DOM attribute
It works, but creates a new handler function on every render
It fires twice per click, once for capture and once for bubble
questions.why: Pass the function (`onClick={handleClick}`) or wrap it (`onClick={() => handleClick(id)}`). As written it runs on every render, and if it sets state that is an infinite render loop.
questions.asked: A junior classic that shows whether JSX expressions are understood as JavaScript.

questions.q: `Counter` keeps a count in state. The user clicks it twice, then `isAdmin` flips. What is the count?
choices: 0, because a different JSX branch creates a new Counter
0, because changing the `label` prop resets its state
2, but only because both branches pass a string label
2, because the same type at the same position keeps state
questions.why: React reconciles by position and type, not by which line of JSX produced the element. Both branches put a `Counter` in the same slot, so React updates its props and keeps its state. Add `key="admin"` / `key="user"` to get separate instances.
questions.asked: It is the mirror image of the key-reset trick, and the bug it causes surprises even experienced developers.

questions.q: What is wrong with this checkbox?
choices: `onChange` fires on blur for checkboxes, so `done` updates late
It is uncontrolled, and `e.target.value` is the string `'false'`
`value` must be a string, so React throws on the boolean `false`
It works, but `e.target.value` lags one render behind the tick
questions.why: A checkbox is controlled with `checked` and read with `e.target.checked`; `value` is only the string submitted with the form. Here the box toggles on its own while `done` becomes the truthy string `'false'`. React's `onChange` fires on every click for checkboxes.
questions.asked: Copying the text-input pattern onto a checkbox is a common bug that reviewers catch.

questions.q: What does `n` show after one click?
questions.why: Updates queue in order: `setN(n + 5)` replaces the value with 5, then the updater receives the queued 5 and returns 6. An updater sees the pending value, while a plain value ignores what came before.
questions.asked: It checks whether you can reason about React's update queue rather than memorise 'use the updater form'.

questions.q: A component increments a module-level `renderCount` variable while rendering. Why is that unreliable?
choices: Module variables are reset each time the component re-renders
Module variables are read-only inside ES module components
React renders components inside a Web Worker, not the page
React may render a component more than once for one commit
questions.why: Rendering must be pure: React can render and discard work (concurrent rendering, StrictMode's double render in development), so side effects during render run an unpredictable number of times. Put side effects in handlers or effects.
questions.asked: Purity of render is the rule concurrent React depends on; interviewers probe it for senior-leaning mid roles.

questions.q: The user types into `Form`, then `showBanner` becomes true. What happens to the typed text?
choices: It is kept, because `false` held the first slot, so `Form` never moved
It is lost, because `Form` moves from the first to the second child
It is lost, because the parent `div` re-renders all of its children
It is kept, but only because `Form` stores its text in an uncontrolled input
questions.why: `{showBanner && <Banner />}` always occupies the first child slot; when false it renders nothing but still counts. So `Form` stays the second child with the same type and keeps its state. Re-rendering is not remounting.
questions.asked: It tests whether you understand how conditional JSX maps to positions in the tree.

questions.q: Why does `<myButton />` render an unknown HTML element instead of your `myButton` component?
choices: Components must be registered with React before JSX can use them
JSX tag names must match the file name the component is exported from
Lowercase JSX tags compile to strings, so they mean HTML elements
Components declared with `function` must be wrapped in `memo` first
questions.why: JSX treats a lowercase tag as the string `'myButton'` (an HTML tag) and a capitalised one as a variable reference. Rename it `MyButton`. There is no registration step in React.
questions.asked: A junior stumbling block that reveals whether JSX compilation is understood.

questions.q: What should a component return to render nothing?
choices: `undefined`, which React forbids and reports as an error
An empty string, which is the only safe empty value
`false` from a class component only, never a function
`null`, which React treats as an empty render
questions.why: Returning `null` is the idiomatic empty render. React 18+ also accepts `undefined`, and `false` renders nothing too, but `null` states the intent. The component still mounts, so its hooks and effects still run.
questions.asked: A quick one; the follow-up about hooks still running separates good answers.

questions.q: In `items.map(item => <Row item={item} />)`, where does the `key` belong?
choices: On the `<li>` that `Row` renders internally, as the list item
On the `<ul>` that wraps the list, so React can track the list
On `<Row>` inside the `map`, the element the array actually holds
On both `<Row>` and its `<li>`, so that each level can be matched
questions.why: Keys identify siblings in the array React receives, and that array holds `<Row>` elements. A key inside `Row` is on a single child, so it does nothing for the list, and React still warns.
questions.asked: It catches people who know keys are needed but not where, a warning seen in most junior code.

questions.q: In React 19 with `createRoot`, how many renders does the timeout callback cause?
choices: One, because React 18+ batches updates from timeouts and promises as well
Two, because batching applies only to updates made inside React event handlers
None until the next user event, because updates outside handlers are queued
Two, because each `useState` setter schedules its own render of the component
questions.why: Automatic batching (React 18+, needs `createRoot`) groups every state update made in the same tick into one render, wherever it came from: timeouts, promises, native listeners. Before React 18 only updates inside React event handlers were batched, which is where the 'two renders' belief comes from. `flushSync` is the opt-out when you need a synchronous render in between.
questions.asked: It checks that 'what changed in React 18' means something concrete to you rather than a release note.

questions.q: What text does this `div` render in React 19?
choices: Nothing: every value in it is falsy
`truefalse0NaN`
`0NaN`
questions.why: React skips booleans, `null`, `undefined` and empty strings, but renders numbers, and `NaN` is a number. That is why `count && <X />` leaks a `0`, and a failed `Number()` parse leaks `NaN`.
questions.asked: It checks you know React's exact rules for falsy children rather than JavaScript's idea of falsy.

questions.q: What happens when this renders?
choices: React throws: `style` must be an object, not a string
The text turns red, exactly as it would in plain HTML
React ignores the prop silently and renders unstyled text
React parses the string into `{ color: 'red' }` for you
questions.why: In JSX `style` takes an object with camelCased keys, as in `style={{ color: 'red' }}`. React 19 throws on a string rather than guessing, so a pasted HTML snippet fails loudly instead of rendering unstyled.
questions.asked: A common slip when pasting HTML into a component; it checks you know JSX is not HTML.

questions.q: `user` is `{ name: 'Ada' }`. What happens when this renders?
choices: It renders `Hello [object Object]`
It renders `Hello Ada` by reading `name`
It renders `Hello` and logs a warning in development
It throws: objects are not valid as a React child
questions.why: React can render strings, numbers, elements and arrays of those, but not plain objects, so it throws 'Objects are not valid as a React child'. Render a field such as `{user.name}` instead. It does not call `toString` for you.
questions.asked: The error message is one every junior meets; interviewers want to hear you would render a field.

questions.q: In React 19, what does `<Badge />` render?
choices: `md`, because `defaultProps` fills in missing props
`undefined`, because 19 ignores it on function components
Nothing: React 19 throws when it sees `defaultProps`
`md` in development, and `undefined` in production
questions.why: React 19 removed `defaultProps` for function components (classes still support it). Use a default parameter, `function Badge({ size = 'md' })`, which is plain JavaScript and works with TypeScript's inference.
questions.asked: Upgrades to 19 break older component libraries on exactly this, so it tests current knowledge.

questions.q: `props` is `{ type: 'email', name: 'e' }`. What `type` does the input get?
choices: `text`, because the later attribute wins
`email`, because spread props always win
Both: React merges them into one attribute
Neither: React throws on duplicate props
questions.why: JSX props are assigned left to right, like object spread, so a prop written after the spread overrides it. Put the spread last if callers should be able to override your defaults, first if your value must win.
questions.asked: Wrapper components live on this rule; it decides whether callers can override your defaults.

questions.q: `count` is already `0`. The user clicks this button three times. How many more times does `Counter` render?
questions.code:
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
return <button onClick={() => setCount(0)}>{count}</button>;
choices: Three: every `setState` call schedules a render
One, for the first click only
Zero: React bails out when the value is unchanged
Six: each click renders once and then commits once
questions.why: React compares the new state with the old using `Object.is`; when they are equal it skips the render. It may occasionally render the component once more before bailing out, but it never re-renders children or runs effects for an identical value.
questions.asked: It checks you understand the bail-out, which is also why mutating state and setting it fails.

questions.q: Why does this link still navigate to `#top` when clicked?
choices: `track()` throws, so React never reaches the `return false`
React ignores the return value; call `e.preventDefault()`
`return false` only works when it is in an `onSubmit` handler
Anchors cannot be prevented; you must render a `<button>` instead
questions.why: Returning `false` from an inline HTML handler cancels the default, but React discards handler return values. Accept the event and call `e.preventDefault()` explicitly.
questions.asked: People coming from jQuery or inline HTML handlers carry this habit into React.

questions.q: What does `e.persist()` do in a React 19 event handler?
choices: It keeps the event alive after the handler, as pooling requires
It stops the event from bubbling to the parent's handlers
It copies the native event, so `e.target` stays valid later
Nothing: React 17 removed event pooling, so it is a no-op
questions.why: Before React 17, synthetic events were pooled and their fields were nulled after the handler, so async code needed `persist()`. Pooling is gone; you can read `e.type` or `e.target` in a `setTimeout` without it, and the method only remains for compatibility.
questions.asked: Old tutorials still show it; knowing why it existed shows you understand synthetic events.

questions.q: While React renders this tree for the first time, which component function is called first?
choices: `Header`, because it is the innermost
Neither: React calls them in parallel
`Page`, which returns the `<Header />` element
Whichever was declared first in the file
questions.why: Rendering is top-down: React calls `Page`, receives an element tree that mentions `Header`, and only then calls `Header`. Effects run in the opposite order, innermost first, which is the pairing people mix up.
questions.asked: It sets up the follow-up about effect order, which runs the other way.

questions.q: Which attribute appears in the DOM?
choices: Only `aria-hidden`, set to `"false"`
Both, each with the value `"false"`
Only `disabled`, set to `"false"`
Neither: `false` removes both attributes
questions.why: `disabled` is a boolean attribute, so React omits it for `false`. `aria-*` and `data-*` attributes are strings, so `false` is written as `"false"`, which for `aria-hidden` is still a valid value. That asymmetry matters for accessibility testing.
questions.asked: It shows you know how JSX maps to real DOM attributes, which matters when debugging a11y.

questions.q: What does React do with this input?
questions.code:
const [email, setEmail] = useState(null);
return <input value={email} onChange={e => setEmail(e.target.value)} />;
choices: Renders it empty and fully controlled from the first render
Renders the text `null` in the field until the user types
Throws, because `value` must never be anything but a string
Treats it as uncontrolled at first and warns about `null`
questions.why: `value={null}` (or `undefined`) means 'uncontrolled', so React warns and then warns again when typing switches it to controlled. Initialise with `''` and keep it a string.
questions.asked: Data loaded from an API with null fields causes exactly this warning on edit forms.

questions.q: What does `Item` render?
choices: `a1`, read from the key
`undefined`, plus a dev warning
Nothing: React throws on `key`
`[object Object]` as text
questions.why: `key` is consumed by React for reconciliation and never passed to the component; reading it gives `undefined` and a warning. Pass the id twice if the child needs it: `<Item key={id} id={id} />`.
questions.asked: It checks you know keys belong to React, not to your component.

questions.q: In a form, what does this button do when clicked?
choices: Runs `clear`, then submits the form and calls `save`
Only runs `clear`, since it has an `onClick`
Runs `save` only, because submit takes priority
Nothing until you add `type="button"` to it
questions.why: A `<button>` inside a form defaults to `type="submit"`, so it runs its click handler and then submits. Give non-submit buttons `type="button"`. React does not change this HTML rule.
questions.asked: The 'why does my Cancel button save the form' bug; the answer is HTML, not React.

questions.q: `<Greeting name="Ada" />` appears in a component's JSX. When does `Greeting`'s function body run?
choices: Immediately, when the JSX expression is evaluated
Only after the parent's effects have finished running
When React renders that element, if it is committed to the tree
Once per module import, and the result is then cached
questions.why: JSX creates a plain object, `{ type: Greeting, props: { name: 'Ada' } }`, without calling `Greeting`. React calls it later while rendering, which is why a created-but-unused element costs almost nothing.
questions.asked: It separates people who know elements are descriptions from people who think JSX calls functions.

questions.q: What goes wrong with `{Header()}` instead of `<Header />`, when `Header` uses hooks?
choices: Nothing: both forms compile to exactly the same element tree
Its hooks become the caller's hooks, so rendering it conditionally breaks
It throws at once, because components cannot be called directly
It renders twice, once as a function and once as an element
questions.why: Calling it as a function runs its hooks inside the parent's render, so React sees them as the parent's hooks and there is no `Header` component in the tree. Rendering it conditionally then changes the parent's hook order, and it gets no identity or state of its own.
questions.asked: It tests whether you know what React means by 'a component', beyond 'a function that returns JSX'.

questions.q: `onChange` on a React text input fires when?
choices: Only once the value is valid for the `type` attribute
Only when the input loses focus, like the DOM `change` event
Only when the user presses Enter inside the field
On every keystroke or edit, like the DOM `input` event
questions.why: React's `onChange` for text fields is wired to the native `input` event, so it fires per edit. That is what makes controlled inputs possible. For blur-time work, use `onBlur`.
questions.asked: It trips people who know DOM events; the React name means something different.

questions.q: Why does this total show `"5"` + `"3"` = `53`?
choices: `type="number"` inputs round-trip through `parseFloat` badly
React converts state to a string when it is rendered
`e.target.value` is always a string, even for number inputs
`useState(0)` fixes the state's type to string after an edit
questions.why: DOM input values are strings regardless of `type`. Convert with `e.target.valueAsNumber` or `Number(...)`, and decide what an empty field means, since `Number('')` is `0`.
questions.asked: A real bug in every quantity field; it checks you think about the DOM's types.

questions.q: Your list keys are `key={Math.random()}`. What is the effect?
choices: Every row remounts on every render, losing state and focus
Nothing visible; random keys just skip the key warning
Rows keep state but React logs a duplicate-key warning
React caches the random key the first time it sees it
questions.why: A new key means a new identity, so React unmounts the old row and mounts a fresh one each render: inputs lose their text and focus, and it is slow. Keys must be stable across renders, not merely unique.
questions.asked: It is the fix people reach for to silence the warning, so interviewers check you know its cost.

questions.q: Two rows in a list accidentally share `key="42"`. What can happen?
choices: React throws and the whole list fails to render
The second row silently replaces the first one on screen
Nothing: React falls back to the array index for both
React logs a warning, and rows may be duplicated or dropped
questions.why: React warns in development, but behaviour is undefined: updates can duplicate or omit rows, and state can attach to the wrong one. Duplicate keys usually mean the data has duplicate ids or two sources were merged.
questions.asked: It usually appears as a production bug; a strong answer traces it back to the data.

questions.q: Two different lists on the same page both use keys `1`, `2`, `3`. Is that a problem?
choices: Yes: keys must be unique across the whole app
No: keys only need to be unique among siblings
Yes, but only when both lists share one parent component
No, as long as both lists use keys of the same type
questions.why: React compares keys only within one parent's children, so separate lists can reuse ids. Siblings in the same array must be unique, so merging two id spaces into one list needs a prefix like `user-1` and `team-1`.
questions.asked: A quick check that you know how far a key's scope reaches.

questions.q: You need a key on each group of `<dt>`/`<dd>` pairs in `items.map`. What do you write?
choices: `<Fragment key={item.id}>` around the pair
`<> key={item.id}` around the pair
`key={item.id}` on the `<dt>` only
A `<div key={item.id}>` around the pair
questions.why: The `<>` shorthand cannot take props, so import `Fragment` and write `<Fragment key={item.id}>`. A wrapping `<div>` would break the `<dl>` markup, and a key on the `<dt>` alone leaves the array's items unkeyed.
questions.asked: It checks both keys and valid HTML, since a stray `div` inside a `dl` is invalid.

questions.q: What is wrong with this component?
choices: `slice` after `sort` returns the lowest three scores
`key={s}` is invalid because keys must be strings
`sort` mutates the parent's array during render
Sorting in render is too slow and belongs in an effect
questions.why: `Array.prototype.sort` sorts in place, so rendering mutates a prop the parent owns, and breaks purity. Use `scores.toSorted(...)` or `[...scores].sort(...)`. Deriving it during render is right; mutating is not. Duplicate scores would also collide as keys.
questions.asked: It checks you spot in-place array methods, which are the commonest purity violation.

questions.q: Which update changes only the user's city without mutating state?
choices: `setUser({ ...user, city: 'York' })`
`setUser({ ...user, address: { ...user.address, city: 'York' } })`
`setUser({ ...user, address: { city: 'York' } })`
`user.address.city = 'York'; setUser({ ...user })`
questions.why: Spread is shallow, so each nested level you change needs its own copy. Replacing `address` with `{ city }` drops `zip`, and assigning to `user.address.city` mutates the old `address`, which earlier renders and memoised children still share.
questions.asked: Nested updates are where immutability is really tested, which is why reducers and Immer exist.

questions.q: Where does React 17+ attach its event listeners?
choices: On each element that has a handler, like `addEventListener`
On `document`, the same as React 16 and every earlier version
On `window`, so events from portals are included too
On the root container you passed to `createRoot`
questions.why: React delegates: one listener per event type on the root container, then it walks the fibre tree to call your handlers. Since 17 that is the root, not `document`, so two React apps on one page, or a React app inside a legacy page, no longer interfere.
questions.asked: It explains odd bugs when mixing React with native listeners, and why 17 changed it.

questions.q: In React 19, a native `document.addEventListener('click', close)` closes a menu. A React `onClick` inside the menu calls `e.stopPropagation()`. What happens when the user clicks in the menu?
choices: `close` still runs, because React listens at `document` itself
`close` runs first, because native listeners always beat React's
`close` does not run: the native event is stopped at the root
`close` runs only in production, where React skips delegation
questions.why: Since React 17, React listens on the root container, so `e.stopPropagation()` stops the native event there, before it bubbles to `document`. Listening at `document` was React 16 behaviour, which is why old click-outside code broke. A capture-phase listener on `document` still fires, because capture runs first.
questions.asked: Click-outside handling is a common exercise, and this is the change that fixed its classic trap.

questions.q: What does `onClickCapture` do differently from `onClick`?
choices: It fires on the way down, before children's `onClick` handlers
It fires only when the click lands exactly on that element
It captures the pointer so drags keep reporting to the element
It fires once per click, even if the element re-renders during it
questions.why: React supports both phases: `onXCapture` runs during the capture phase, from the root down, so a parent sees the event before any child's bubbling handler. It is useful for logging or blocking clicks inside a region.
questions.asked: It checks that you know the DOM event model applies in React too.

questions.q: Why does this JSX not compile?
choices: `<Spinner />` needs a `return` in front of it
`loading` must be a boolean to use `if` in JSX
Conditionals must live in a separate component
Braces take expressions; `if` is a statement
questions.why: JSX braces hold a JavaScript expression, because JSX compiles to function arguments. Use `loading && <Spinner />`, a ternary, or an `if` before the `return` that assigns to a variable.
questions.asked: A syntax question that shows whether you understand what JSX compiles to.

questions.q:
Why must a component's JSX have a single root, as in `return <>

`?
choices: The DOM refuses to insert two sibling nodes at once
A component returns one value, and JSX is a function call
React can only diff trees that have exactly one root node
Keys cannot be assigned to more than one returned element
questions.why:
`

` would be two expressions side by side, like `return f() g()`. Wrapping them in a fragment makes one value without adding a DOM node. Returning an array also works but needs keys.
questions.asked: An opener that shows whether you know JSX is JavaScript, not markup.

questions.q: Which is the idiomatic way to render nothing when `items` is empty and a list otherwise?
choices: `{items.length > 0 && <List items={items} />}`
`{items.length && <List items={items} />}`
`{!!items && <List items={items} />}`
`{items ?? <List items={items} />}`
questions.why: An explicit boolean keeps `0` off the page. `!!items` is always true for an array, empty or not, and `??` only checks for `null` or `undefined`, so it returns the array itself.
questions.asked: A quick check that you would not ship the stray-zero bug.

questions.q: A child component edits its `items` prop with `props.items.push(newItem)`. What goes wrong?
choices: It throws, because props objects are frozen in production
Nothing, as long as the parent re-renders at some point later
It mutates the parent's state, and React will not re-render for it
React copies props per child, so only the child's copy changes
questions.why: Props are references to the parent's data; pushing mutates the parent's state array in place, with no render and a later surprise. Props are read-only: ask the parent to change the data through a callback such as `onAdd(item)`.
questions.asked: It is 'props are read-only' made concrete, which is a stronger answer than reciting the rule.

questions.q: In development, `props` objects are frozen in React 19. What does that change for a child that does `props.title = 'x'`?
choices: It succeeds, and the parent sees the new title
It throws a TypeError in strict-mode JavaScript
React silently rolls the change back after render
It succeeds in development but fails in production
questions.why: React freezes the props object in development, and ES modules run in strict mode, so assigning to a frozen property throws. That catches the mistake early. Nested objects inside props are not frozen, so `props.user.name = 'x'` still mutates silently.
questions.asked: A detail that shows you have met the error, and know the nested case still slips through.

questions.q: What does `setCount` return?
choices: The new state value
The previous state value
A promise for the render
`undefined`
questions.why: Setters return nothing; the new value appears on the next render. If you need the new value now, compute it into a variable, then both use it and pass it to the setter.
questions.asked: Short, and it leads into the 'state is a snapshot' follow-up.

questions.q: Why does a click handler that reads `count` right after `setCount(count + 1)` see the old value?
choices: The setter is asynchronous and returns a promise you forgot to await
React batches the call, and it lands after the event loop finishes
`count` is a constant for that render; the new value is the next render's
`setCount` only writes to the DOM; state catches up in an effect
questions.why: Each render gets its own `count`, a plain `const` captured by the handler. Calling the setter schedules a new render with a new `count`; it cannot change the variable you already hold. 'Async' is the wrong mental model, since awaiting would not help.
questions.asked: The strong answer is 'snapshot', not 'async'; interviewers listen for that word.

questions.q: When is it fine to read `window.innerWidth` directly during render?
choices: In a client-only app, if you do not need updates on resize
Always, because render runs in the browser
Never: reading any global breaks the rules of React
Only inside `useMemo`, so it is cached
questions.why: Reading it gives the value at render time but will not re-render on resize, and it fails during server rendering where `window` is undefined. To track it, subscribe with `useSyncExternalStore` or an effect.
questions.asked: It checks whether you know what makes a value reactive in React.

questions.q: Which is a valid React component name?
choices: `profileCard`
`user-card`
`user_card`
`UserCard`
questions.why: JSX treats a capitalised tag as a variable reference and lowercase as an HTML tag, and hyphens are not valid in identifiers. `<userCard />` would create an unknown `usercard` element.
questions.asked: Warm-up level; it leads into what JSX compiles to.

questions.q: `Counter` shows 2. Then `fancy` becomes true. What does it show?
choices: 2, because `Counter` is the same component
0, because its parent's element type changed
2, but only if `Counter` is wrapped in `memo`
0, because every conditional remounts its branch
questions.why: React matches by type at each position. When `div` becomes `section`, React tears down that whole subtree, including `Counter`'s state. Swapping only `className` on the same `div` would keep it.
questions.asked: It checks you know state belongs to a position in the tree, not to a component name.

questions.q: `Counter` shows 1. Then `fancy` becomes true. What does it show?
choices: 1: the same types sit at the same positions
0: the two JSX branches are separate elements
0, because a changed `className` remounts the div
1, but only because both branches are on one line
questions.why: Both branches describe a `div` containing a `Counter` at the same position, so React updates the `className` and keeps the `Counter`. The two branches being different JSX expressions does not matter; only the resulting tree does.
questions.asked: Paired with the type-change case, it shows you reason from the tree rather than from the code.

questions.q: Rows use `key={index}` and each holds an uncontrolled `<input>`. The user types into row `a`, then `z` is added at the start. Where does the typed text appear?
choices: In the row labelled `a`, which moved down
Nowhere: every row remounts and is cleared
In the row labelled `z`, now in first position
In both the `z` and `a` rows, duplicated
questions.why: Key `0` used to be `a` and is now `z`, so React keeps the first `<li>` and its input and just changes the label. The typed text stays at position 0, next to the wrong item. A stable `key={it.id}` moves the input with its row.
questions.asked: This is the demonstration interviewers want when you say 'index keys are bad'.

questions.q: `name` changes from 'Ada' to 'Bob' after mount. What does the input show?
choices: 'Bob', because the prop changed
'Ada', because `defaultValue` is read only once, on mount
An empty field, because React clears it on the change
'AdaBob', because React appends the new default value
questions.why: `defaultValue` sets the initial value of an uncontrolled input; after mount the DOM owns it. To load a new record into an uncontrolled form, remount it with `key={record.id}`, or make the field controlled.
questions.asked: Edit forms that load late hit this; the fix tells the interviewer whether you know about keys.

questions.q: What does `items` contain after one call to `add`?
questions.why: Both calls build from the same snapshot, the empty `items`, and the second replaces the first. Use `setItems(prev => [...prev, x])` whenever an update builds on the previous array.
questions.asked: The array version of the double-increment question; it shows whether the idea transfers.

questions.q: A button rendered through `createPortal` into `document.body` is clicked. Does the `onClick` on the `div` that renders the portal fire?
choices: No: the button is not inside the `div` in the DOM
Only if the portal target is inside the `div`
Yes: React events bubble through the React tree
Only for events that do not bubble natively
questions.why: Synthetic events follow the component tree, not the DOM tree, so a click in a portal reaches React ancestors. That is convenient for modals, and surprising when a parent's `onClick` closes something.
questions.asked: Modal bugs come from this, and it shows you know the React tree and DOM tree can differ.

questions.q: React throws 'Element type is invalid: expected a string ... but got: undefined'. What is the usual cause?
choices: An import is wrong, e.g. named versus default export
A component returned `undefined` instead of `null`
A list item is missing its `key` prop entirely
A hook was called conditionally inside a component
questions.why: The component you rendered is `undefined`, which almost always means `import Widget from` a file that only has `export function Widget`, or the reverse, or a typo in the name. Returning `undefined` from a component is allowed in React 18 and later.
questions.asked: A debugging question: can you map a cryptic error to its everyday cause?

questions.q: `Show` reads `useContext(Theme)`, where `Theme = createContext('light')`, but no provider is above it. What does it get?
choices: `undefined`
`null`
An error: missing provider
`'light'`
questions.why: The argument to `createContext` is the value used when no provider is found. Many teams pass `null` and throw in a custom `useTheme()` hook, so a missing provider fails loudly instead of silently using a default.
questions.asked: Short, and it leads into why custom context hooks often throw on a missing provider.

questions.q: What does `Show` render?
choices: `dark`, the outermost provider's value
`blue`, the nearest provider's value
`dark blue`, both values joined
The context's default value
questions.why: `useContext` reads the closest provider above the component, so inner providers override outer ones. That is how you theme one section of a page differently. React 19 lets you render `<Theme>` directly as the provider.
questions.asked: It checks the lookup rule that makes nested providers useful.

questions.q: What CSS does React write for `style={{ width: 100, lineHeight: 2 }}`?
choices: `width: 100px; line-height: 2`
`width: 100px; line-height: 2px`
`width: 100; line-height: 2`
It throws: numbers need units
questions.why: React appends `px` to numbers except for unitless properties such as `lineHeight`, `zIndex`, `opacity` and `flex`. For other units, pass a string like `'1rem'`.
questions.asked: A detail you only know if you have written inline styles in React.

questions.q: What text does this paragraph produce?
choices: `Hello world`, with a space
`\n Hello \n world`
`Helloworld`, with no space
`Hello  world`, with two spaces
questions.why: JSX trims text at line breaks and drops lines that are only whitespace, unlike HTML, which collapses the newline to a space. Add `{' '}` where you want a space between the text and the element.
questions.asked: A small bug that ships to production, and it shows you know JSX whitespace rules differ from HTML.

questions.q: How do you make a `<select>` controlled in React?
choices: Put `selected` on the chosen `<option>`
Pass `value` and `onChange` to the `<select>`
Pass `defaultValue` to the chosen `<option>`
Call `select.value = x` in an effect
questions.why: React moves the selected value to the `<select>` itself, like a text input. Setting `selected` on options triggers a warning. For `multiple`, `value` is an array.
questions.asked: It checks you know React normalises the form elements.

questions.q: How do you set a controlled `<textarea>`'s text in React?
choices: Put the text between the tags, as in HTML
Use `defaultValue` together with `onChange`
Use `innerText` in a ref after the mount
Use `value` and `onChange`, like an input
questions.why: React treats `<textarea>` like `<input>`: `value` for controlled, `defaultValue` for uncontrolled. Children are not supported. `defaultValue` with `onChange` is still uncontrolled.
questions.asked: Warm-up that confirms you know the form-element rules.

questions.q: Which renders a controlled radio group for `size`?
choices: `<input type="radio" value={size} onChange={...} />` on each
`<input type="radio" selected={size === 'm'} />` per option
`<input type="radio" checked={size === 'm'} onChange={...} />` per option
`<input type="radio" defaultChecked={size} />` on the first one
questions.why: Radios and checkboxes are controlled through `checked`, not `value`. Each radio's `value` names the option, and `onChange` sets `size` from `e.target.value`.
questions.asked: Everyone does text inputs; radios show whether you know the rule generalises through `checked`.

questions.q: After an upload finishes, the user picks the very same file again and the input's `onChange` never fires. Why, and what is the usual fix?
choices: The value is unchanged, so no change event fires; clear it with `e.target.value = ''`
React dedupes identical `File` objects; wrap `upload` in `useCallback` to reset it
The browser caches the file handle; set `e.target.files = null` inside the handler
`onChange` fires only once per mount; give the input `key={Date.now()}` on each render
questions.why: The browser fires `change` only when the selection differs, and picking the same file leaves it identical. Setting `value` to an empty string is the one write scripts may make to a file input, so clear it after reading `files` (or remount the input with a new `key` once, after the upload). A key that changes on every render would remount it constantly.
questions.asked: Shows you have actually shipped an upload form and know the browser rule behind the bug.

questions.q: In an `onSubmit` handler, why use `new FormData(e.currentTarget)` rather than `e.target`?
choices: `e.target` is `null` for submit events in React
`currentTarget` includes disabled fields; `target` does not
`FormData` refuses to accept `e.target` in React 19
`currentTarget` is always the form the handler is on
questions.why: `currentTarget` is the element the handler is attached to; `target` is where the event came from. For submit they are usually the same, but in TypeScript `currentTarget` is typed as `HTMLFormElement` and it is the right habit for bubbling events.
questions.asked: It checks event basics and hints at TypeScript experience with form handlers.

questions.q: Why store `selectedId` in state instead of a copy of the selected item object?
questions.code:
const [items, setItems] = useState(initial);
const [selected, setSelected] = useState(null); // an item
choices: Objects cannot be stored in React state reliably
An edit to `items` leaves the stored copy stale
Ids render faster than objects in JSX
`useState` compares objects by value, not by reference
questions.why: Two copies of the same item drift apart: rename it in `items` and `selected` still shows the old name. Keep the id and derive `items.find(i => i.id === selectedId)` during render; there is one source of truth.
questions.asked: It is the 'avoid duplicated state' principle applied to a case everyone has built.

questions.q: A fetch screen keeps `isLoading`, `isError` and `data` in three `useState` calls. What is the design problem?
choices: It allows impossible combinations, e.g. loading and error
Three setters cause three separate renders each time
Booleans cannot be used as state in React components
`data` must be fetched inside the `isLoading` setter
questions.why: Nothing stops `isLoading && isError` both being true after a missed reset. A single `status: 'idle' | 'loading' | 'error' | 'success'` makes invalid states unrepresentable, which TypeScript can then enforce.
questions.asked: Interviewers use this to see if you design state or just add booleans until it works.

questions.q: Where should `fullName` come from?
questions.code:
const [first, setFirst] = useState('');
const [last, setLast] = useState('');
choices: A third state, updated in both `onChange` handlers
An effect that sets it whenever `first` or `last` change
A `const` computed during render: `${first} ${last}`
A ref, so updating it never causes an extra render
questions.why: Anything you can compute from existing state or props should be computed during render. A third state can drift, and an effect adds a render with the stale value first.
questions.asked: The simplest form of 'don't store what you can derive'.

questions.q: Two sibling `Panel`s should never be open at the same time. What is the idiomatic structure?
choices: Each `Panel` keeps `isOpen` and closes the other through a ref
The parent holds `openId`; each `Panel` gets `isOpen` and `onOpen`
A module-level variable tracks which of the panels is open
Each `Panel` reads the other one's state via context
questions.why: The rule involves both panels, so the state lives in their common parent. Panels become controlled: they show `isOpen` and ask to change it through `onOpen`. Refs and globals bypass React's rendering, so the screen can go out of sync.
questions.asked: An accordion is the textbook lifting-state exercise, and interviewers like it as a live task.

questions.q: `show` goes from true to false and back to true. What is `Counter`'s count?
choices: What it was before, as React caches it
Undefined until `Counter` sets it again
Whatever the last render of the parent had
Its initial value, since it unmounted
questions.why: Rendering `false` removes `Counter` from the tree, and React discards its state. When it comes back it is a new instance. To keep state while hidden, keep it mounted and hide it with CSS, use `<Activity>` in 19.2, or lift the state up.
questions.asked: It checks the basic mount/unmount lifecycle of state before the harder identity questions.

questions.q: A tab panel must keep its form input when the user switches tabs and back. Which approach does NOT keep it?
choices: Keep every panel mounted and hide the inactive ones with CSS
Wrap each panel in React 19.2's `<Activity mode="hidden">`
Render only the active panel with `{active === 'a' && <A />}`
Lift the form's values up into the parent that owns the tabs
questions.why: Conditional rendering unmounts the inactive panel and loses its state. Hiding keeps it mounted, `<Activity>` keeps state while hidden (and pauses its effects), and lifting keeps the values outside the panel.
questions.asked: It turns 'unmounting loses state' into a design choice with trade-offs.

questions.q: `Counter` appears twice on the page. The user clicks the first one. What happens to the second?
choices: Nothing: each instance has its own state
It increments too; they share one state
It resets to zero after the click
It increments only if the two are siblings
questions.why: State belongs to a position in the tree, so each rendered instance gets its own. Sharing needs the state lifted to their common parent and passed down.
questions.asked: A warm-up that confirms you know state is per instance.

questions.q: Which lists more state than this search screen needs?
choices: Only `query`, since `allUsers` itself should be in state
Only `count`, since `results` is needed for the filter
None: each value appears on screen, so each needs state
Only `query`, since `results` and `count` can be derived from it
questions.why: With `allUsers` already available, `results` is a filter of it by `query`, and `count` is `results.length`. Storing them means every `setQuery` must remember to update both, and one day it will not.
questions.asked: Minimal state is the core idea of 'Thinking in React', and this is how it is examined.

questions.q: When is copying a prop into state, as in `useState(props.initialColor)`, the right design?
choices: Never: every prop copied into state is a bug
When the prop is only an initial value and later changes should be ignored
When the prop is an object, so React can compare it by value
Whenever the child needs to read the prop inside an effect
questions.why: Seeding state from a prop is fine when that is the intent, and the `initial` or `default` name says so. It is a bug when the child is meant to follow the prop, because later changes are ignored.
questions.asked: A nuanced version of 'don't mirror props', and nuance is what mid-level interviews reward.

questions.q: What is the difference between a controlled and an uncontrolled component, in one sentence?
choices: Controlled gets its value from props or state; uncontrolled keeps it internally
Controlled uses hooks; uncontrolled uses classes
Controlled validates input; uncontrolled accepts anything the user types
Controlled renders on the server; uncontrolled only renders in the browser
questions.why: The distinction is who owns the value. A controlled component gets `value` and reports changes; an uncontrolled one, like a plain `<input defaultValue>`, keeps its own and you read it when needed. The idea applies to your components too, not just inputs.
questions.asked: It is asked verbatim; the strong answer generalises beyond `<input>`.

questions.q: A large settings form only needs its values on submit. What does an uncontrolled form with `FormData` save you?
choices: All validation, which the browser then handles alone
The need for a `name` attribute on each form field
A state variable and re-render per field on every keystroke
Server-side validation, which is no longer required
questions.why: Uncontrolled fields keep their values in the DOM, so typing does not re-render the form, and `new FormData(form)` reads them all on submit. You lose instant derived UI, such as live previews; that is when controlled fields earn their cost.
questions.asked: It checks you choose between controlled and uncontrolled on purpose, not by habit.

questions.q:
In `
    {users.map(u => )}
`, what happens without a `key`?
choices: It fails to compile until you add one
It renders, warns, and matches rows by position
It renders with each user's `id` used automatically
It renders, but React re-mounts every row each time
questions.why: Without keys React warns and falls back to the index, with all its reordering bugs. It does not look for an `id` field or remount everything.
questions.asked: The follow-up to 'what is key for', to check you know what happens without one.

questions.q: `users` has already been fetched. Which way of showing active users follows React's model?
choices: Keep `active` in a ref and refill it in each click handler
`useEffect(() => setActive(users.filter(...)), [users])`
Filter them in the fetch callback and store both arrays
`const active = users.filter(u => u.active)` in the body
questions.why: A filtered list is derived data, so compute it during render; if it is genuinely expensive, wrap it in `useMemo`. The effect version renders once with stale data, and two stored arrays can disagree.
questions.asked: It is the 'you might not need an effect' idea in its most common form.

questions.q: What is a 'pure' component in React's sense?
choices: One that renders HTML elements only, never other components
One wrapped in `React.memo`, so that it never re-renders
Same props, state and context in, same JSX out, with no side effects
One with no state of its own, only props from its parent
questions.why: Rendering must be a calculation: no mutation of existing values, no requests, no timers. Side effects belong in event handlers or effects. Purity is what lets React render twice, pause or discard a render safely.
questions.asked: Purity underpins StrictMode, concurrency and the Compiler, so interviewers check you can define it.

questions.q: Which line breaks render purity?
choices: A
B
C
D
questions.why: Line C mutates a prop during render, a side effect on data the parent owns. Reading and computing, as in A and B, is fine; record views in an effect or event handler instead.
questions.asked: Spotting side effects in render is a core code-review skill.

questions.q: How is the virtual DOM diff kept fast enough, given that a general tree diff is O(n³)?
choices: Heuristics: other types replace a subtree, and keys match siblings
React diffs only the parts of the tree that are visible on screen
Web workers compute the diff off the main thread in the background
The browser does the diffing natively via `document.diff()`
questions.why: React assumes elements of different types produce different trees, so it replaces rather than compares them, and it matches siblings by key instead of trying every pairing. That makes reconciliation roughly linear.
questions.asked: It separates people who can explain reconciliation from people who say 'the virtual DOM is fast'.

questions.q: React splits an update into render and commit phases. What happens in the commit phase?
choices: Your components are called to produce new JSX
React compares the old and new state values
React fetches any data that the components need
React applies the DOM changes, then runs effects
questions.why: Render calls components and works out what changed; it has no visible effect and can be paused or thrown away. Commit applies the changes to the DOM in one go, attaches refs, then runs layout effects and later passive effects.
questions.asked: It checks that 'render' means calling your component, not updating the screen.

questions.q: A parent re-renders, and `Child`'s props are identical. Does `Child` re-render by default?
choices: No: React skips children with unchanged props
Yes: children re-render unless memoised
Only when `Child` has state of its own
Only when the props are objects
questions.why: By default a render cascades to every child. React only skips when the child is wrapped in `memo` and its props are shallow-equal, or when the element object itself is the same, as with `children`. Re-rendering is usually cheap; the DOM only changes if the output differs.
questions.asked: The most common misconception about rendering; it sets up the memo discussion.

questions.q: What does `flushSync(() => setOpen(true))` from `react-dom` do?
choices: Applies the update and commits the DOM before it returns
Batches the update with any others pending in this tick
Sends the update to the server in a synchronous request
Delays the update until the browser is next idle
questions.why: It forces React to render and commit synchronously, so the next line can measure or focus the new DOM. It is an escape hatch; overusing it defeats batching and hurts performance.
questions.asked: A rare but real tool; knowing it exists, and why it is rare, signals depth.

questions.q: What does this list render when `items` is `["a", "b"]`?
choices: Two `<li>` elements, because `map` returns each JSX value
An empty `<ul>`: the arrow body has braces but no `return`
A compile error, because JSX cannot sit inside a block body
A key warning and two `<li>` elements rendered by position
questions.why: With braces the arrow is a block body, so each callback returns `undefined` and React renders nothing for those holes. Drop the braces or write `return <li ...>`. The JSX inside is a legal expression statement, so it compiles fine.
questions.asked: A classic "why is my list empty" bug; strong candidates spot it from the braces alone.

questions.q: What does `Stars` render for `<Stars count="3" />`?
choices: `4`, because JSX converts numeric-looking strings
`31`, because a quoted prop is always a string
`NaN`, because a string prop cannot be added to
A type error thrown during render in development
questions.why: Quoted attribute values are string literals, so `"3" + 1` concatenates to `"31"`. Pass numbers, booleans and objects in braces: `count={3}`. React never coerces prop types for you.
questions.asked: Checks you know the difference between a string attribute and a JavaScript expression in JSX.

questions.q: What does `Modal` receive as `open` in `<Modal open />`?
choices: The string `"open"`, as in HTML
`undefined`, because no value was given
`true`, as a boolean shorthand
An empty string, like an HTML attribute
questions.why: A JSX attribute with no value is shorthand for `={true}`. HTML treats a bare attribute as present with an empty string value, which is the misconception the other choices lean on.
questions.asked: Quick warm-up; the follow-up is usually how you pass `false` (`open={false}` or omit it).

questions.q:
`bio` comes from the API as `"Hi there"`. What does `

{bio}

` show?
choices: "Hi" in bold, followed by " there"
Nothing at all, because React strips unknown markup
An error that strings cannot contain markup
The literal text `Hi there`, tags and all
questions.why: React escapes strings rendered as children, so markup appears as text and cannot inject script. Rendering HTML needs `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` plus sanitising. Nothing is stripped or rejected.
questions.asked: Links JSX to XSS: the strong answer says escaping is the default and HTML injection is opt-in.

questions.q: `remove(id)` deletes a row. What does it receive when the button is clicked?
choices: The row id, taken from the closest `key` prop
`undefined`, as React calls handlers with no arguments
The button's DOM node, bound as the first argument
The click event object, not an id
questions.why: React calls the handler with the synthetic event, so `remove` gets an event where it expected an id. Wrap it: `onClick={() => remove(row.id)}`. Keys are never passed to handlers or components.
questions.asked: Very common junior bug; the follow-up is why `onClick={remove(row.id)}` is wrong too.

questions.q: Clicking a row opens its detail page. Clicking the row's Delete button deletes it but also opens the detail page. What is the usual fix?
choices: Call `e.stopPropagation()` in the Delete handler
Call `e.preventDefault()` in the Delete button handler
Move the row handler to `onClickCapture`
Return `false` from the Delete handler
questions.why: React events bubble through the component tree, so the row's `onClick` runs after the button's. `stopPropagation` stops that. `preventDefault` only cancels default browser actions, capture would run the row handler first, and returning `false` does nothing in React.
questions.asked: Tests bubbling versus default actions, which candidates often mix up.

questions.q: What happens when `<Greeting name="Ada" />` renders?
choices: It renders "Hi Ada", since the only prop is passed
It renders "Hi " because `name` is `undefined` there
It throws: `name` is the props object, not a string
It renders "Hi [object Object]" as plain text
questions.why: A component receives one argument, the props object, so `name` is `{ name: "Ada" }`. Rendering a plain object as a child throws "Objects are not valid as a React child". Destructure: `function Greeting({ name })`.
questions.asked: Checks you know components take a single props object; destructuring is the idiom.

questions.q:
Why does React ask for keys in `items.map(...)` but not for `
  • A
  • B
`?
choices: Static siblings get their keys added by the JSX compiler
Static children have fixed positions, so position is identity
Keys matter only when a list has more than a few items
Literal `<li>` elements are skipped by reconciliation
questions.why: Hand-written siblings can never be reordered or removed between renders, so their position is a stable identity. An array can change shape, so React needs keys to match items. The compiler adds no keys, and length has nothing to do with it.
questions.asked: Shows you understand what keys are for rather than reciting "lists need keys".

questions.q: State is `{ name: "Ada", email: "" }`. What is the state after this call?
choices: `{ name: "Ada", email: "ada@x.io" }`, merged
`{ email: "ada@x.io" }`, with `name` gone
`{ name: "Ada", email: "" }`, unchanged
An error, as the shape must match the initial state
questions.why: A `useState` setter replaces the value; it never merges. Spread the old state: `setForm({ ...form, email })`. Class components' `this.setState` did merge shallowly, which is where the belief comes from.
questions.asked: A frequent source of "my other field vanished" bugs when moving from classes to hooks.

questions.q: An old tutorial mounts the app with `ReactDOM.render(<App />, el)`. What happens in React 19?
choices: It works but logs a deprecation warning
It renders in legacy, non-concurrent mode
It is quietly redirected to `hydrateRoot`
It fails: the API was removed in React 19
questions.why: `ReactDOM.render` and `hydrate` were deprecated in 18 and removed in 19; use `createRoot(el).render(<App />)`. React 18 still ran it in legacy mode with a warning, which is the behaviour the distractors describe.
questions.asked: Shows you are current with React 19 and can migrate old entry points.

questions.q: Why do some older files start with `import React from "react"` even though they never mention `React`?
choices: JSX used to compile to `React.createElement`
Hooks fail without the default import in scope
Bundlers tree-shake React unless it is imported
The import registers the file as a component
questions.why: The classic JSX transform turned `<div />` into `React.createElement(...)`, so `React` had to be in scope. The automatic runtime (React 17+) imports `jsx` from `react/jsx-runtime` itself, so the import is unnecessary now.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know JSX is compiled, and by what.

questions.q: A form has ten text inputs in one `form` state object. What is the idiomatic single change handler?
choices: Read `e.target.id` and look the field up in a large `switch`
Give each input a `ref` and read them all on every change
Use `name` and `setForm({ ...form, [e.target.name]: e.target.value })`
Call `new FormData(e.target)` and replace the whole state object
questions.why: Each input's `name` matches a key, and a computed property updates just that key while the spread keeps the rest. A `switch` repeats ten cases, and `FormData` on an input element is not how it works (it takes a form).
questions.asked: Everyday CRUD form code; interviewers like the computed-key answer.

questions.q: In React 19, what does `<div class="card" />` do?
choices: It throws, because `class` is a reserved word
It renders with no class attribute at all
It sets `class="card"` and logs a dev warning
It compiles to `className` silently, no warning
questions.why: React passes it through, so the DOM gets `class="card"`, but warns "Invalid DOM property `class`. Did you mean `className`?". JSX is JavaScript, so `className` (and `htmlFor`) is the correct prop name; `class` as an attribute name is legal syntax.
questions.asked: Everyone knows "use className"; the strong answer explains why and what really happens.

questions.q: A `Heading` takes `level` from 1 to 6. Which renders the right tag?
choices: `const Tag = "h" + level; return <Tag>{children}</Tag>;`
`return <h{level}>{children}</h{level}>;` as a JSX template
`return <heading level={level}>{children}</heading>;`
`const el = "h" + level; return <el>{children}</el>;`
questions.why: JSX treats a capitalised name as a variable, and a string variable renders that DOM tag. A lower-case `tag` is read as the literal element `<tag>`, and `<h{level}>` is not valid syntax.
questions.asked: Dynamic tags come up in design-system work; tests the capitalisation rule.

questions.q: `icons` maps names to components. Why does `<icons[kind] />` fail to compile?
choices: Components cannot be stored in plain objects and looked up
`kind` must be declared with `const` to be used
Object keys must be capitalised to be used as tags
JSX tag names cannot be computed member expressions
questions.why: JSX allows dotted names like `<icons.Check />` but not bracket access. Assign first: `const Icon = icons[kind]; return <Icon />;`. Storing components in objects is fine.
questions.asked: Comes up when mapping a status to an icon; the fix is a capitalised local variable.

questions.q: A `Button` accepts an `icon` prop. The caller writes `icon={StarIcon}`. How must `Button` render it?
choices: `{icon}`, since a component renders when used as a child
`{icon()}`, calling it like a helper
`const Icon = icon; <Icon />` before rendering
`{React.cloneElement(icon)}` to create a copy
questions.why: A component function passed as a value must be rendered as an element; assign it to a capitalised name first. `{icon}` renders nothing useful (functions are not valid children), calling it bypasses hooks rules, and `cloneElement` needs an element such as `icon={<StarIcon />}`.
questions.asked: Tests the element-versus-component distinction, which matters in every design-system API.

questions.q: A button contains an `<svg>` icon. The user clicks the icon. Which is the button inside the button's `onClick`?
choices: `e.target`, always the element that owns the handler
`e.currentTarget`, the element the handler is on
`e.relatedTarget`, set for clicks that hit children
`e.nativeEvent.target`, React's own button reference
questions.why: `e.target` is where the click happened, here the `svg` or its `path`; `e.currentTarget` is the element whose handler is running. Reading `e.target.dataset` in such a handler is a classic intermittent bug.
questions.asked: The icon-in-button bug is common; the strong answer names both properties.

questions.q: What does `<Size size={null} />` render?
choices: `md`, because the default covers any empty value
`null`, because defaults apply only to `undefined`
Nothing, because a `null` prop removes the element
`undefined`, because `null` props are dropped
questions.why: Destructuring defaults fire only when the value is `undefined`. `null` is a real value, so it passes through. Callers who mean "use the default" should omit the prop, or the component should use `size ?? "md"`.
questions.asked: Default props now live in destructuring; this checks the `null` edge case.

questions.q: What does React do with `className={isActive && "active"}` when `isActive` is `false`?
choices: Sets `class="false"` on the element
Sets an empty `class=""` attribute
Omits the attribute and logs a dev warning
Throws because `className` must be a string
questions.why: React drops `false` for a non-boolean attribute and warns "Received `false` for a non-boolean attribute". Write `className={isActive ? "active" : undefined}` or use a class-joining helper. It does not stringify to "false".
questions.asked: Shows attention to warnings; many codebases have this exact pattern.

questions.q: How do you set a CSS custom property from props?
choices: `style={{ accent: color }}`, and React adds the `--` prefix
`style={{ "--accent": color }}`, used with `var(--accent)` in CSS
`style="--accent: red"` as a plain CSS string
`data-accent={color}` read by CSS `attr(data-accent)`
questions.why: React passes keys that start with `--` to `style.setProperty`, so custom properties work in the style object. A string `style` throws, React never adds prefixes, and `attr()` for non-content properties is not usable across browsers yet.
questions.asked: Theming components with CSS variables is common; this checks the exact syntax.

questions.q: Which inserts `item` at index `i` of `items` state without mutating it?
choices: `setItems(items.splice(i, 0, item))`
`items.splice(i, 0, item); setItems([...items])`
`setItems(items.toSpliced(i, 0, item))`
`setItems([items.slice(0, i), item])`
questions.why: `toSpliced` (ES2023) returns a new array and leaves the old one alone. `splice` mutates and returns the removed elements, copying afterwards still mutated state first, and the last choice nests an array instead of spreading it.
questions.asked: Checks you know the non-mutating array methods, not only `map` and `filter`.

questions.q: What is wrong with this toggle?
choices: Nothing: the spread made the change completely safe
It mutates the todo object shared with the old array
`setTodos` ignores arrays that keep the same length
The spread breaks the keys of every row in the list
