questions.why: Spreading copies the array, not the objects in it, so `next[0]` is the same object the previous state holds. Memoised rows and anything comparing old and new items then see no change. Replace the item: `todos.map(t => t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)`.
questions.asked: The shallow-copy trap; strong candidates explain which references changed and which did not.

questions.q: You want to keep a callback in state. What does this click store?
choices: The arrow function itself, ready to be called later on
`undefined`: React calls it as an updater and stores the result
`null`, because `useState` rejects functions as values
A bound copy of the function, re-created on every render
questions.why: A function passed to a setter is treated as an updater `prev => next`, so React calls it (logging "done" immediately) and stores its return value, `undefined`. Wrap it: `setOnDone(() => () => console.log("done"))`, or keep callbacks in a ref.
questions.asked: Deep check on the updater overload; it bites people building modal and toast APIs.

questions.q: During its render, `Child` calls a setter it received from `Parent`. What happens?
choices: React throws an error and unmounts both of the components
The update is silently ignored until the next user event
React warns about updating another component mid-render
It works and is the idiomatic way to report values up
questions.why: Rendering must be pure, so updating another component mid-render is flagged; React still applies it and re-renders `Parent`, which can loop. Compute the value in `Parent`, or report it from an event handler. Setting your own state during render is the only allowed form, for adjusting state to props.
questions.asked: Checks you know the render phase must not cause side effects on other components.

questions.q: Why does this form still reload the page on submit?
choices: `preventDefault` runs after an `await`, once the default action has happened
React ignores `preventDefault` when it is called inside an async function handler
`onSubmit` needs `e.stopPropagation()` as well to cancel the reload
Forms reload unless their submit button has `type="button"` on it
questions.why: The browser decides on the default action as soon as the handler returns synchronously, and an async function returns at its first `await`. Call `e.preventDefault()` first, then await. `stopPropagation` affects bubbling, not the default action, and a `type="button"` button would not submit at all.
questions.asked: Async submit handlers are everywhere; this ordering bug is easy to write and hard to spot.

questions.q: A "Clear" button calls `formRef.current.reset()` on a form of controlled inputs. What happens?
choices: The inputs clear, and React updates state to match
React throws, because `reset` is blocked on controlled forms
The inputs clear in the DOM, while state keeps the old values out of sync with them
The inputs stay as they are, since state still holds the values
questions.why: `reset()` restores default values in the DOM, but React re-applies each controlled `value` from state, so nothing visible changes. Reset the state instead (`setForm(initial)`). With uncontrolled inputs, `reset()` does work.
questions.asked: Tests that you know who owns the value in a controlled input.

questions.q: A text input has the `required` attribute and the user submits it empty. What happens to the form's React `onSubmit`?
choices: It runs, and `e.target.validity.valid` is `false` inside it
It runs only when `noValidate` is also set on the input
It does not run: the browser blocks submission and shows a message
It runs twice: once to validate the fields and once for the actual submit
questions.why: Native constraint validation happens before the `submit` event fires, so an invalid form never reaches `onSubmit`. Add `noValidate` on the form if you want to run your own validation UI instead. The server must still validate.
questions.asked: Checks you can use the platform's validation instead of reinventing it.

questions.q: How do you read the chosen values from a `<select multiple>` in `onChange`?
choices: `e.target.value`, which is an array when `multiple` is set
`e.target.values`, a React-only property for multi-selects
`Array.from(e.target.selectedOptions, (o) => o.value)`
`e.target.value.split(",")`, since values are comma-joined
questions.why: A multi-select's `value` is still just the first selected option; `selectedOptions` lists them all. In React you control it with an array: `<select multiple value={tags}>`. There is no `values` property and no comma joining.
questions.asked: A less common control that shows whether you know the DOM API underneath React.

questions.q: The input shows "12". The user types "a". What does the input show afterwards?
choices: "12a", until the next render corrects it
An empty string, because the test failed
"a", because the newest keystroke replaces the value
"12", because React restores the controlled value
questions.why: After the event, React sets the DOM value back to state, and state is still "12", so the keystroke is rejected. This is how a controlled input filters input. Note that `type="text"` with `inputMode="numeric"` is usually better than this for numbers on phones.
questions.asked: Shows you understand that state is the source of truth for a controlled input.

questions.q: A form's `onSubmit` calls `save(data)` but never calls `e.preventDefault()`. What does the user see?
choices: The save runs, and the page stays as it is
The browser navigates, reloading the page
React prevents the default for you in forms
A console warning, then the save as normal
questions.why: Without `preventDefault`, the browser performs a normal form submission to the `action` URL (the current page by default), so the page reloads and in-flight requests may be cancelled. React 19 prevents the default only when you pass a function to the `action` prop.
questions.asked: The most common first-form bug; mentioning the React 19 `action` exception adds depth.

questions.q: A popover should close when focus leaves it. Why does the container's React `onBlur` fire when the user tabs between two buttons inside it?
choices: React `onBlur` bubbles like `focusout`; check `e.currentTarget.contains(e.relatedTarget)`
The inner buttons steal the event, so attach `onBlur` to each inner button instead of the container
It is a React bug; use a native `blur` listener, which bubbles correctly
Focus moves through `body` between elements, so the popover truly loses it
questions.why: React's `onFocus`/`onBlur` are built on `focusin`/`focusout`, which bubble, so the container hears every child blur. `relatedTarget` is the element receiving focus: if the container contains it, focus stayed inside. Native `blur` does not bubble at all.
questions.asked: Real bug in menus and comboboxes; the relatedTarget check is the strong answer.

questions.q: In React 17 and later, a parent has `onScroll` and a child list scrolls. Does the parent's handler run?
choices: Yes, all React events bubble through the tree
Only if the child also has an `onScroll` prop
No, React stopped bubbling `onScroll` in 17
Only in `onScrollCapture`, never in `onScroll`
questions.why: Native scroll events do not bubble, and React 17 changed `onScroll` to match, so a parent only hears its own element scrolling. Attach the handler to the scrolling element. Most other React events, including focus events, still bubble.
questions.asked: Deep event-system detail; comes up when building infinite scroll or sticky headers.

questions.q: What does this log when the user types into the input?
choices: Nothing: forms have no change event in React
`undefined`, because the target is the form
`email`, since React `onChange` bubbles up
Nothing until the input loses focus, then `email`
questions.why: React `onChange` on inputs fires per keystroke and bubbles, so a form-level handler sees every field's change with `e.target` being the input. Some form libraries rely on this. The "only on blur" behaviour is the native `change` event, which React does not use for text inputs.
questions.asked: Checks you understand React's `onChange` is not the DOM `change` event.

questions.q: How should a search input run `search()` when the user presses Enter?
choices: `onKeyPress` checking `e.charCode === 13` on the input
`onKeyDown` checking `e.key === "Enter"`, or wrap it in a form
`onChange` checking whether the value ends in a newline
`onKeyUp` checking `e.keyCode === 13`, which also covers older browsers
questions.why: `keypress`, `charCode` and `keyCode` are deprecated; `e.key` is the modern API. Better still, put the input in a `<form>` and handle `onSubmit`, which gives you Enter for free. Text inputs never contain newlines.
questions.asked: Checks for current event APIs and the "use a form" instinct.

questions.q: Users add todos by typing text; the todos have no id. Where should each row's `key` come from?
choices: Generate `crypto.randomUUID()` in the `map` callback
Use the array index, since new todos go at the end
Assign an id with `crypto.randomUUID()` when the todo is created
Use `todo.text` as the key, since users rarely type the same todo twice
questions.why: The id must be stable across renders, so create it once, when the item is created, and store it with the item. Generating it in `map` gives a new key every render and remounts every row. Text can repeat and indexes break on delete or reorder.
questions.asked: The strong answer is about when the id is created, not which function makes it.

questions.q: Rows are keyed by `id` and each has an uncontrolled `<input>`. The user types into row B, then the list is re-sorted so B moves to the top. Where is the typed text?
choices: In the new top row, which is B
In the second row, where B used to be
Gone, because sorting remounts every row
In both rows, until the next render
questions.why: With stable keys React moves the existing DOM node and its state with the item. This is exactly what index keys break: with `key={i}` the text would stay at position two and appear to jump rows.
questions.asked: Pairs with the index-key bug; being able to predict both outcomes is the point.

questions.q: An app calls `root.render(<App theme="dark" />)` again on the root it already rendered `<App theme="light" />` into. What happens?
choices: The old tree is unmounted, and `App` mounts fresh with the new prop
It throws, because a root can only render once
Two copies of `App` render inside the container
React reconciles and updates `App`, keeping its state
questions.why: A second `render` on the same root is just another update: same component type at the same position, so state is preserved and only the prop changes. Use `root.unmount()` to tear down. This is how non-React pages sometimes drive an embedded React widget.
questions.asked: Shows you understand roots and reconciliation beyond the default one-line entry point.

questions.q: In React 19, a page component renders `<title>Orders</title>` inside its `<main>`. Where does the title element end up?
choices: In `document.head`, setting the tab title
Inside `<main>`, where it has no effect
Nowhere, React strips unsupported tags
In `<head>`, but only with a helmet library
questions.why: React 19 hoists `<title>`, `<meta>` and `<link>` rendered anywhere in the tree into `document.head`, so components can own their metadata. Before 19 you needed a library such as react-helmet or had to set `document.title` in an effect.
questions.asked: A visible React 19 change; interviewers use it to check how current you are.

questions.q: In React 19, what happens to `items={[1, 2]}` on a defined custom element `<my-list>`?
choices: It becomes the attribute `items="1,2"`, as React always did
React assigns it to the element's `items` property
It is dropped, because custom elements accept only strings
React throws because arrays are not valid attribute values
questions.why: React 19 fully supports custom elements: when the element defines a property of that name, React sets the property, so objects and arrays arrive intact. React 18 stringified everything into attributes, which is why web components felt awkward in React.
questions.asked: Relevant when integrating design systems built as web components.

questions.q: A function component still declares `Card.propTypes = { title: PropTypes.string }`. What does React 19 do with it?
choices: Checks props in development, as before
Ignores it: propTypes checks were removed
Throws at startup until it is deleted
Checks it in production builds only, for speed
questions.why: React 19 removed propTypes checking (and `defaultProps` for function components); the property is simply ignored. Type props with TypeScript, and validate external data at runtime with a schema library.
questions.asked: Common in migrations; the good answer names TypeScript as the replacement.

questions.q: In React 19, `profile.website` is the string `"javascript:alert(1)"`. What does `<a href={profile.website}>` produce?
choices: A working `javascript:` link, since React trusts attribute values
A link whose `href` React replaced with one that throws when used
No `href` at all, with a warning about invalid URLs in development
An escaped `href` that the browser treats as a relative path
questions.why: React 19 blocks `javascript:` URLs by swapping in a URL that throws "React has blocked a javascript: URL as a security precaution". Still validate user URLs on the server and allow only `http(s):`. React 16.9–18 only warned.
questions.asked: User-supplied links are a real XSS vector; knowing React's guard and its limits is strong.

questions.q:
In a client-side React 19 app, what is wrong with `async function Profile() { const u = await getUser(); return

{u.name}

; }`?
choices: Nothing: React 19 awaits async components on the client
Async components are for Server Components only; React warns on the client
It needs a surrounding `<Suspense>` boundary; with one, it works in every environment
`await` is fine, but the component must then return a Promise of null
questions.why: Only Server Components may be async functions. On the client React warns that async/await is not supported in Client Components, and the component can re-suspend forever because each render makes a new promise. Fetch in an effect, a query library, or pass a cached promise to `use()`.
questions.asked: Checks that you do not blur Server and Client Components together.

questions.q: `Tooltip` renders its content through `createPortal` into `document.body`. Does that content see the `ThemeContext` provider wrapping `Tooltip`?
choices: No, context follows the DOM tree
Only if the provider wraps `body` too
Only with a second provider in the portal
Yes, context follows the React tree
questions.why: A portal changes where the DOM nodes go, not where the component sits in the React tree, so context (and event bubbling) works as if it rendered in place. That is what makes portals practical for modals and tooltips.
questions.asked: Checks the React-tree versus DOM-tree distinction.

questions.q: Tabs are hidden with `style={{ display: active ? "block" : "none" }}` instead of `{active && <Tab />}`. What changes?
choices: Hidden tabs stay mounted and keep their state
Nothing, both unmount the hidden tab
Hidden tabs keep DOM nodes but lose their state
Hidden tabs re-mount each time they are shown
questions.why: CSS hiding keeps the component mounted, so input text and scroll position survive, at the cost of rendering all tabs and running their effects. Conditional rendering unmounts and resets. React 19.2's `<Activity mode="hidden">` gives a middle ground.
questions.asked: A design trade-off question: keep state versus render cost.

questions.q: A handler calls `setItems([...items])` with no other change. Does the component re-render?
choices: No, React compares the array contents first
Yes, because it is a new array reference
No, because the length did not change
Only if an item object itself was replaced
questions.why: React compares state with `Object.is`, which checks references. A fresh array is a different reference even with identical contents, so React re-renders. The reverse bug, mutating and passing the same array, skips the render.
questions.asked: The reference-equality rule underlies every "why did/didn't it update" question.

questions.q: A list keeps `selection` in state and must clear it whenever the `items` prop changes. Which approach does the React docs recommend over an effect?
choices: This one: adjust state during render when a prop changes
A `useEffect` on `[items]` that calls `setSelection(null)`
A `useMemo` on `[items]` that returns a fresh selection
A `ref` that stores `items` and clears on each render
questions.why: Setting your own state during render makes React discard the JSX and re-render immediately, before the screen or children see stale selection. An effect paints once with the stale value first. Often better still is a `key` on the list, or storing only a selected id and deriving the rest.
questions.asked: An advanced alternative to effects; knowing when to prefer a key shows judgement.

questions.q: A React component shows a status by running `document.getElementById("status").textContent = "Saved"` in a click handler. What is the problem?
choices: Nothing, as long as the element has a unique id on the page
React owns that DOM; the next render can overwrite the text
The call throws because React hides the real DOM from you
It is only a problem on the server, where `document` is missing
questions.why: React renders DOM from state; a manual edit is invisible to it, so the next render of that node puts React's version back, or React may even crash when the DOM no longer matches. Keep "Saved" in state and render it. Direct DOM access is legal, just not for content React manages.
questions.asked: The declarative-versus-imperative question in its simplest form.

questions.q: Which JSX sets these HTML attributes correctly?
choices: `<label for="e" dataTestid="lbl" tabindex={0}>`, as in HTML
`<label htmlFor="e" dataTestId="lbl" tabIndex={0}>`
`<label for="e" data-testid="lbl" tab-index={0}>`
`<label htmlFor="e" data-testid="lbl" tabIndex={0}>`
questions.why: Reserved words and most attributes use their DOM property names (`htmlFor`, `tabIndex`), but `data-*` and `aria-*` stay hyphenated exactly as in HTML. camelCasing a data attribute renders an unknown attribute instead.
questions.asked: A quick syntax check; the `data-`/`aria-` exception is what separates answers.

questions.q: How do you write a comment inside JSX children?
choices: `<!-- note -->`, as in HTML
`// note` on its own line
`# note` after the tag
questions.why: Children are text or `{expressions}`, so a comment must live inside braces as a block comment. An HTML comment renders as literal text or fails to parse, and `//` inside children is just text.
questions.asked: Warm-up syntax; also checks you know JSX is not HTML.

questions.q: `<Button onClick={save} />` renders a custom `Button`. Why does clicking it do nothing?
choices: `onClick` is just a prop; `Button` never passes it on
Custom components need `onPress`, not `onClick`
Events on custom components need `useCallback`
React binds `onClick` only on native tags, and only at first mount
questions.why: On a component, `onClick` is an ordinary prop with no built-in meaning. `Button` must forward it: `<button onClick={onClick}>`, or spread the rest of its props onto the element. Only DOM elements attach event listeners.
questions.asked: Checks the difference between DOM elements and components.

questions.q: A form uses a fixed list of 200 countries that never changes. Where should that list live?
choices: In `useState`, so the dropdown can re-render with it
In a module-level constant outside the component
In a `useEffect` that fills a state variable on mount
In a ref, so it is not re-created on every render
questions.why: Data that never changes and does not depend on props or state is not state at all. A module constant is created once and shared. State or an effect adds renders for nothing; a ref works but only hides the same constant behind indirection.
questions.asked: Tests the "what is actually state" instinct.

questions.q: Why does the counter stay at 0 on screen?
choices: `count` should be `var`, so its value survives renders
The arrow function captured a copy of `count`, so the variable itself never changes
Numbers in JSX must be wrapped in `String()` to update
A local variable changes but does not trigger a render, and resets each call
questions.why: Changing a local variable does not tell React to re-render, and each render calls `Counter` again, which re-declares `count = 0`. State is what persists between renders and schedules one. The closure does see the variable; it just does not matter.
questions.asked: The first "why do we need state" question in many screens.

questions.q:
While `user` is still `undefined` (loading), what does `

{user.name}

` do?
choices: It renders an empty paragraph until the data arrives, then fills it in
Throws a TypeError, crashing the tree up to an error boundary
Renders the text "undefined" in the paragraph
Skips this render and waits for the next one
questions.why: Reading a property of `undefined` throws during render; without an error boundary the whole root unmounts. Guard it: `user?.name`, an early `if (!user) return <Spinner />`, or model a loading status explicitly.
questions.asked: Loading states are where most blank-page crashes come from.

questions.q: A component re-renders after a state change. What happens to its DOM?
choices: React rebuilds that component's entire DOM subtree from scratch
The whole page's DOM is diffed against a saved HTML copy
React compares the new output and patches only what changed
Nothing, until the browser's next repaint requests a copy
questions.why: Rendering produces new elements, which React reconciles against the previous ones, then commits only the needed DOM changes. That is why input focus and scroll survive re-renders. A render is not a DOM rebuild.
questions.asked: Checks that "re-render" is understood as "call the function again", not "redraw everything".

questions.q: How do you give an uncontrolled checkbox an initial ticked state?
choices: `checked={true}` with no `onChange`
`defaultChecked={true}`
`value="on"` on the input
`defaultValue={true}`
questions.why: `defaultChecked` sets the starting state and leaves the DOM in charge afterwards. `checked` without `onChange` makes a read-only controlled box (with a warning), and `defaultValue`/`value` set the submitted value, not the ticked state.
questions.asked: Checks the default-versus-controlled prop pairs for checkboxes.

questions.q: A reviewer says `onClick={() => select(id)}` "creates a new function on every render, so it is slow". What is the accurate reply?
choices: Creating a small function is cheap; it matters only for memoised children
True; always wrap handlers in `useCallback` to avoid it
True; move the handler outside the component to fix it
False; React caches inline arrow functions between renders automatically
questions.why: Allocating a closure costs next to nothing. A new function identity only matters when it is passed to a `memo` child or used as an effect dependency, and then `useCallback` (or the React Compiler) helps. React does not cache inline functions itself.
questions.asked: Tests for cargo-cult optimisation versus an understanding of when identity matters.

questions.q: In a class component, state is `{ name: "Ada", age: 36 }`. What is it after `this.setState({ age: 37 })`?
choices: `{ age: 37 }`, like a `useState` setter would store
`{ name: "Ada", age: 37 }`, merged shallowly
`{ name: "Ada", age: 36 }` until `forceUpdate()` runs
An error: class state must be replaced as a whole
questions.why: Class `setState` shallow-merges the object into the existing state; the `useState` setter replaces it. Only the top level merges, so nested objects still need spreading. Legacy code relies on this difference.
questions.asked: Legacy class code is still common; this checks you can switch mental models.

questions.q: In a class component, `onClick={this.handleClick}` throws "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'setState')". Why?
choices: Class methods cannot call `setState` from event handlers
`handleClick` must be declared `static` to be used in JSX
React calls event handlers with `this` set to the clicked DOM element
The method is passed unbound, so `this` is `undefined` when called
questions.why: Passing `this.handleClick` detaches the method, and class bodies are strict mode, so `this` is `undefined` when React calls it. Bind in the constructor or declare it as an arrow class field: `handleClick = () => {...}`. React does not set `this` to the element.
questions.asked: A classic `this` question dressed as React; legacy codebases still have it.

questions.q: A `Card` spreads all props onto its `<div>`: `<div {...props}>`. A caller passes `isActive`. What happens?
choices: The div gets a lower-cased `isactive` attribute, and nothing is logged
React silently drops every prop that is not a valid attribute
React warns that it does not recognise `isActive` on a DOM element
The component throws, since camelCase attributes are invalid
questions.why: React warns about unknown camelCase props on DOM elements (and about non-string values). Destructure what the component uses and spread only the rest: `const { isActive, ...rest } = props`. React does not validate or strip unknown props for you.
questions.asked: Wrapper components leak props this way; the destructure-then-spread idiom is the answer.

questions.q: `List` does `children.map(...)`. It works with two `<li>` children but throws "children.map is not a function" with one. Why?
choices: React converts one child to a string before passing it on
Children are frozen objects, so `.map` is removed in dev
A single child is passed as the element itself, not an array
A single child turns `children` into a Set, which has no `map` method
questions.why: `children` is opaque: an array for several children, a single element for one, and `undefined` for none. Use `Children.map` / `Children.toArray`, or better, accept an explicit array prop such as `items`.
questions.asked: Checks you know `children` has no fixed shape.

questions.q: `SearchBox` renders `<input value={value} onChange={(e) => onChange(e.target.value)} />`. Typing does nothing. What is the likely cause?
choices: The parent's `onChange` does not update the state it passes as `value`
`onChange` must receive the event, not `e.target.value`, to work
Controlled inputs need a `defaultValue` as well as a `value` to accept typing
The input must own a `useState` copy of `value` to be editable
questions.why: A controlled child shows exactly what the parent passes. If the parent's handler logs but never calls its setter (or updates the wrong field), `value` never changes and every keystroke is reverted. Copying the prop into child state creates two sources of truth.
questions.asked: Tests debugging of the controlled-component data flow.

questions.q: `Counter` holds its own count. What happens when the first button is clicked?
choices: Each button shows 1, since the two are one shared instance
React throws, since an element cannot be rendered twice
Each button shows 1 after a second render, once they sync up
Only the first shows 1: each position is its own instance
questions.why: An element is only a description; state belongs to the position in the tree where it is rendered. Rendering the same element object twice creates two independent `Counter` instances. Reusing element objects is allowed.
questions.asked: Separates elements (descriptions) from instances (state holders).

questions.q: One click calls a setter in `Parent` and a setter in `Child`. How many render passes does React 19 do?
choices: Two: one for each component that has new state queued
One: updates from the same event are batched together
Three: parent, child, then the parent again
Two in development and one in production
questions.why: React batches every update queued during one event, across components, and renders them in a single pass from the top, so `Child` renders once with both changes. Batching is not per component.
questions.asked: Checks that batching is understood as per event, not per component.

questions.q: In React 19 development, with `<StrictMode>`, a component's `console.log("render")` appears twice on mount, the second one greyed out. Why?
choices: React calls it twice to expose impure rendering, then discards one result
React renders twice and keeps the second result
The component mounted twice because the root was accidentally created twice
The log is echoed by DevTools; the component rendered only once
questions.why: Strict Mode double-invokes component bodies in development to surface side effects in render. React 19 dims the second call's logs in the console. Production renders once, so never rely on the count.
questions.asked: Usually asked as "why does my component log twice?"; naming dev-only and purity is the answer.

questions.q: To toggle one flag, a handler does `const next = structuredClone(state); next.rows[5].open = true; setState(next)`. What is the cost?
choices: None: a full deep copy is the textbook way to do an immutable update
Every object gets a new identity, so memoised rows all re-render
It mutates `state`, because `structuredClone` is shallow
It fails, because React state cannot be structured-cloned
questions.why: Deep-cloning copies the whole tree, and every unchanged row becomes a new object, which defeats `memo` and reference checks everywhere. Immutable updates should copy only the path to the change and share the rest. `structuredClone` is deep, not shallow.
questions.asked: Tests understanding of structural sharing, not just "do not mutate".

questions.q: Why did React 18 remove the "Can't perform a React state update on an unmounted component" warning?
choices: Setting state after unmount now throws an error instead of logging a warning
React 18 keeps unmounted components alive, so the update applies
It mostly flagged harmless cases, like a fetch finishing after unmount
The warning moved into the ESLint plugin as a lint rule
questions.why: The update is a no-op; the warning pushed people into `isMounted` workarounds that fixed nothing. Real leaks come from subscriptions or timers never cleaned up, which effect cleanups solve. Nothing throws and nothing is kept alive.
questions.asked: Shows you know why `isMounted` flags are an anti-pattern.

questions.q: A controlled input's `onChange` awaits a formatter and only then calls `setValue`. What goes wrong while typing?
choices: Nothing; React waits for the promise before painting
The input becomes uncontrolled and React logs a warning
Every keystroke is applied twice, once now and again when the promise settles
React reverts the keystroke first, so the caret can jump to the end
questions.why: After the event, React restores the DOM to the current state, erasing the keystroke; when state catches up later, the value is replaced and the caret moves to the end. Update state synchronously in `onChange` and do async work separately.
questions.asked: A subtle but real bug; explaining the revert-then-replace sequence is the strong answer.

questions.q: Why do `Children.toArray(children)` elements have keys like `.0` and `.$x`?
choices: They are React's internal fiber ids, exposed for debugging
They are random keys that change on every call to `toArray`
They are HTML ids added to the DOM so testing libraries can find each child
It assigns keys from position or existing key so the array can be re-rendered
questions.why: `toArray` prefixes each child's key: position-based (`.0`) for unkeyed children and escaped (`.$x`) for keyed ones, so you can sort or slice the array and still render it without key warnings. Keys never reach the DOM.
questions.asked: Rare in app code but common in library code reviews.

questions.q: A controlled `<select value={country}>` receives `"zz"`, which matches no `<option>`. What happens?
choices: React adds a hidden option so the value is kept
The browser shows the first option while state still says "zz"
React throws an invalid-value error during render
The select shows a blank value and state quietly resets to an empty string
questions.why: The DOM cannot select a missing value, so it falls back to the first option. State and UI now disagree, and submitting without a change sends "zz" from state but the user saw another country. Include a placeholder option for empty or unknown values.
questions.asked: An easy way to ship wrong data; the placeholder option is the fix to mention.

questions.q: `Table` defines `const Row = memo(RowView)` inside its own body. What happens to each row's state when `Table` re-renders?
choices: It is reset: every render creates a new `Row` type, so rows remount
It is preserved, and `memo` even skips the row renders
It is preserved, because the wrapped `RowView` itself stays the same function each time
It is reset only for rows whose props have changed
questions.why: React matches by element type, and `memo(...)` inside the body returns a new component each render, so every row unmounts and mounts again, losing state and focus. Call `memo` at module level. The wrapped function being the same does not help.
questions.asked: The "optimisation" that makes things worse; tests type identity.
